title: How Pinball Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and mechanics of pinball. They trace its roots to the nineteenth-century Bagatelle table, the 1930s explosion of pinball innovations (coin operation, bumpers, tilt, scoring) and the Chicago-centered industry, then the introduction of flippers with Gottlieb's Humpty Dumpty in 1947 and Spot Bowler in the 1950s. They cover the anti-pinball laws (LaGuardia's New York ban, the Pearl Harbor-era raids, pinball hidden in pornography shops), Roger Sharp's 1976-era city council demonstration that saved the game, the decline after video games, Pinball 2000, Stern as the remaining maker, and the modern collector and home market. The second half explains how pinball works: playfield, flippers, ball, plunger or solenoid, back glass, black box, electro-mechanical parts, scoring and combination shots, multiball, replays, match, and the tilt and slam tilt mechanisms. The episode ends with listener mail about a doctor's response to patients who bring in lint and hair as supposed parasites, and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with light banter about Las Vegas and pinball machines.

segments.title: Bagatelle table and early pinball origins
segments.summary: The hosts trace pinball to nineteenth-century Bagatelle tables, and Montague Redgrave's addition of a spring-loaded ball shooter in the 1930s. Early play was coin-free and bought from a ball keeper.

segments.title: 1930s pinball innovation and the Great Depression
segments.summary: The 1930s brought a wave of innovations, including coin operation, bumpers, tilt, electric circuits, legs, and scorekeeping. Cheap pinball became popular during the Depression, and the number of manufacturers fell from 145 in the early thirties to fourteen by the mid-thirties, with Chicago as the center.

segments.title: Pinball collecting and the hosts' personal experiences
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh discuss playing pinball at Chuck's brother's game room, which holds several machines and a retro arcade conversion, and their favorite eras and games, including Adams Family Pinball.

segments.title: Flippers arrive and pinball becomes a game of skill
segments.summary: Before flippers, players could only nudge the machine, so the game was closer to chance. Gottlieb's Humpty Dumpty in 1947 is credited as the first modern game with flippers, and the 1950s Spot Bowler had the first modern flipper arrangement. The early flippers were shorter and faced the opposite way.

segments.title: Pinball bans and LaGuardia's crackdown
segments.summary: Pinball was outlawed in most major US cities, with the ban in New York justified as gambling. Mayor LaGuardia ordered raids, including right after Pearl Harbor, when machines were smashed and dumped in the river. From the forties to the mid-seventies, play was often limited to back rooms of pornography shops.

segments.title: Roger Sharp saves pinball at the City Council hearing
segments.summary: Pinball's legality was debated at a New York City Council hearing. Roger Sharp, a pinball expert, demonstrated skill on an unfamiliar backup machine and made a center-aisle shot. The council then repealed the ban. The hosts also mention Oakland overturning its pinball ban and Sharp's sons who rank among top players.
topics: New York City Council pinball hearing

segments.title: Decline, Pinball 2000, and the modern pinball market
segments.summary: Pinball declined after video games arrived. Bally and Williams produced Pinball 2000, a hybrid with video screens that was not popular. Stern became the sole major maker, then competition came from Jersey Jack Pinball. The modern market is driven by home collectors and imports from overseas.

segments.title: Pinball anatomy: playfield, flippers, ball and plunger
segments.summary: The hosts explain the basics: the playfield, bottom flippers, upper flippers, the ball (steel, about 1 and 1/16 inches, around 2.8 ounces, up to 90 mph), magnets and vortex features, and ceramic Powerballs. The plunger or solenoid launches the ball.

segments.title: Scoring, combination shots, multiball, replays and match
segments.summary: Scoring involves combination shots and game-within-a-game modes, using High Roller Pinball as an example, with Casino Frenzy and wizard modes. Multiball is described, and free games come from replay thresholds or the match feature.

segments.title: Back glass, black box, electro-mechanical parts and tilt
segments.summary: The back glass and black box house electronics, while most mechanical functions remain electro-mechanical. The wooden playfield is tilted about six to seven degrees. The tilt mechanism uses a swinging ballast and copper ring, with two warnings before flippers stop, and a slam tilt shuts the game down.

segments.title: Listener mail: doctor on lint and hair as parasites
segments.summary: A listener shares a doctor's Facebook comment about patients who bring in lint and hair as suspected parasites or eggs and bugs, explaining why antiparasitic treatment is avoided without evidence and why the patient's experience still matters. The hosts thank listeners.
